feedback: If the child travels across the floor or steps sideways instead of pivoting, mark the spot with a hoop or footprints and require both feet to stay put while turning to face a named target.

If the finish facing is a random amount (not toward the named target), give fixed facings to turn TO — door then window — so a quarter turn lands on a checkable target rather than reteaching the whole idea; the concept may well be held, with only the execution lacking a reference point.
When two quarter turns leave them facing the opposite way, name it: 'two quarter turns make a half turn.'
activities.intendedInsight: A turn is an amount of rotation about a fixed point, felt in the body — not travelling. A quarter turn lands you on a new facing (about 90° from the start), a half turn faces you the opposite way, a three-quarter turn is three quarter-turns on, and a whole turn returns you to the same facing.
learnerActions: Stand on a marked spot (hoop or footprints) with both feet staying put throughout the turn.
Mark your start facing (e.g. 'I'm facing the door'), then make a quarter turn to your right and name your new facing ('now the window').

Go back to your start facing (the door). Make a half turn and check you are facing the opposite way from the start; go back to the start facing, make a whole turn and check you are facing the same way as the start.

Go back to your start facing, then make a three-quarter turn to your right and check where you now face (three quarter-turns to the right from the start, the same facing as one quarter turn to the left).
Make two quarter turns in a row in the same direction (both to the right) and compare: is that the same as one half turn?
activities.title: Turn your whole body on the spot

feedback: If the route is only 'go forward' steps with the turns left out, walk their exact words back to them so they SEE the path miss the bookshelf (or hit a wall), then have them re-give it including the turns.

If they turn the wrong way, reinforce body left/right (e.g. a sticker on the right hand) and keep up exposure; do not drill it as a failure — frame-dependent left/right matures later, especially after they have turned to a new facing or face a partner.
activities.intendedInsight: A followable route is a coordinated sequence of moves AND turns with correct directional words — leaving out the turns breaks the path. Giving a route (not just following one) shows the directional words have become a productive tool.
learnerActions: Follow a spoken route given by an adult or partner: 'go forward two, turn left a quarter, go forward one.'
Then GIVE directions yourself: describe how to walk from here to the bookshelf as a sequence of moves and turns.
Have your listener walk your exact words — if they miss the bookshelf or hit a wall, find the missing or wrong move or turn and re-give the route.
Try describing the route for walking backward from the bookshelf to the start.
activities.title: Give and follow a route

feedback: When the robot misses the goal, point to the arrow's facing after the turn and ask which turn was the wrong amount or direction.
If a quarter turn does not land 90° on, let the child re-enter the command and re-run it so the correction is immediate and visible.
activities.intendedInsight: A 'quarter turn' only makes sense as landing on a new facing toward the next target, and the order of turning and walking matters: turn-then-walk is different from walk-then-turn.
learnerActions: On a floor grid or maze, string commands for a character/robot: 'forward 2', 'turn left a quarter', 'forward 1'.
Aim the robot at a goal; if a turn is the wrong direction or amount, the robot faces the wrong way and misses or runs into a wall.
Watch the start and finish facings shown as an arrow, and adjust so a quarter turn visibly lands the arrow 90° on.
Compare turning-then-walking with walking-then-turning and notice the different results.
activities.title: Program a robot along a floor grid (companion)
